items.summary: We examine the role of the compact Lie group $SO(3)\times O(2)$ in the metric critical-point theory of normalized thick knots. The quotient by this group is part of the construction of ropelength-filtered knot spaces, but passage to an orbit space need not preserve the weak-slope notion of criticality. We establish elementary structural results for the action, including finiteness of isotropy for nontrivial knot types and exact invariance of the descending strong slope under a compact isometric quotient. We give counterexamples, including one with the connected group $SO(2)$, showing that the analogous assertion for the weak slope fails in general. On the other hand, we prove that it does hold, up to a multiplicative constant, at every point where the orbit map admits a Lipschitz local section together with a continuous gauge, and we construct such data for normalized thick knots from finitely many Fourier modes. Consequently, on the open stratum of thick knots with trivial isotropy, weak-slope criticality on the parametrized model and on the quotient coincide; at a configuration with nontrivial finite isotropy $\Gamma$ we show that finitely many Fourier modes recover $\Gamma$ exactly, and that the comparison problem is equivalent, up to constants, to the same problem for the finite group $\Gamma$ acting on a slice. For the unknot the round circles, whose isotropy is $O(2)$, remain outside this reduction. We also show that configurations whose thickness is not saturated have descending strong slope at least $2\pi/(\pi+1)$. For closed subgroups we define symmetry-constrained connected and path minimax levels and prove attainment of finite connected merge levels from compact sublevels; a finite-dimensional example, computed exactly, demonstrates a strict symmetry-breaking minimax gap. Finally we distinguish these static statements from Noether conservation laws for a separately specified dynamics.

items.summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. Development repository: https://github.com/BioDecodingLab/Physically_Constrained_Representations_of_Active_Matter

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: The magnetotelluric (MT) method uses natural electromagnetic field variations to image subsurface electrical resistivity at depths ranging from tens of metres to hundreds of kilometres. It is widely used in geophysical exploration for natural resources, including minerals, geothermal energy, and groundwater, as well as in the characterisation of sites for CO$_2$ storage and in studies of crustal and lithospheric structure. The MT inverse problem is, however, inherently non-unique: many distinct resistivity models reproduce the observations equally well. Conventional practice nonetheless reports a single regularised model, with no quantitative measure of its uncertainty. MTGeophysics.jl is a Julia package developed to address this limitation. Its principal aim is the quantification of uncertainty in MT model building, advancing interpretation from a single deterministic model, through an ensemble of plausible models, towards the full posterior distribution. The package also provides tools for data analysis, mesh generation, masking, forward modelling, inversion, model analysis and visualisation for MT research and applications. This paper studies how they fit together, one layer at a time. Its two-sided Kleisli category is the category of Markov kernels indexed by a source, with one source held throughout a composite. Marginalisation is total and affine. Event conditioning is partial and nonlinear. It is undefined exactly where the event has probability zero, it cannot be extended continuously to that wall, and its derivative grows like 1/p(A) near it. Conditioning commutes with marginalisation only for events that are cylinders over the kept coordinates. Contextual Bayes decomposition. It commutes with every window, but it is not injective: two families of sources can share a pooled law and every pooled table while differing in every labelled table. Step 2, the tangent layer. The cone tangent structure of the tangent companion commutes with the provenance comonad. items.summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: The magnetotelluric (MT) method uses natural electromagnetic field variations to image subsurface electrical resistivity at depths ranging from tens of metres to hundreds of kilometres. It is widely used in geophysical exploration for natural resources, including minerals, geothermal energy, and groundwater, as well as in the characterisation of sites for CO$_2$ storage and in studies of crustal and lithospheric structure. The MT inverse problem is, however, inherently non-unique: many distinct resistivity models reproduce the observations equally well. Conventional practice nonetheless reports a single regularised model, with no quantitative measure of its uncertainty. MTGeophysics.jl is a Julia package developed to address this limitation. Its principal aim is the quantification of uncertainty in MT model building, advancing interpretation from a single deterministic model, through an ensemble of plausible models, towards the full posterior distribution. The package also provides tools for data analysis, mesh generation, masking, forward modelling, inversion, model analysis and visualisation for MT research and applications. Physical experiments are proposed only for enclosed small-scale test beds, certified material coupons, hardware-in-the-loop fleet schedules and independently metered docking stations. No integrated public-road vehicle, passenger application, vehicle type approval or automatic nano-to-car scale transfer is asserted. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen distributed cooperative exchange architecture against competent fixed-body fleet dispatch, centralized modular scheduling and metered teleoperated docking with the same material, energy, operator, station, sensing, communication and computation resources. A proposed service advantage must survive the entire population of requested jobs and attempted exchanges. The source's selective-risk model, R_sel(tau) = E[L(yhat,y) given c >= tau], is retained but always reported together with accepted-task coverage; refusing difficult requests cannot count as safety or efficiency progress. Hidden donated-module withdrawals, false connector capability, overloaded docking, station closures, common-reference localization bias, message partitions, unfair task selection and an unavailable external safety referee are active attempts to refute the central claim. Loss of load path, physically unqualified attachment, forbidden traffic clearance or untraceable authorization is an immediate hard stop. Each plate supplies a physical or mathematical construction, units and validity assumptions, a concrete blinded falsifier and linked study chapters. An algorithmic objective does not replace independent mechanical evidence or human authority. Eighty-two chapters and 410 individual single-page research studies examine physical cooperative missions, donor-recipient interfaces, distributed reservations, convoy dynamics, fleet optimization, human supervision, independent metrology and cross-generation research succession. items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .
